title: The apocalypse in art
hook: the Angers tapestry, Dürer's woodcuts: artists pictured Revelation vividly
tomorrow: When the saints go marching in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dates people set for the end, and Jesus's plain words about that day. Your line was no one knows the hour. What fear did you set down on the table? Day one thousand three hundred eighteen.

In a castle in the French city of Angers hangs a tapestry of the book of Revelation, woven in wool, so long that you see it by walking beside it, scene after scene: angels with trumpets, the dragon, the beast, the holy city coming down. In Germany, the artist Albrecht Dürer made Revelation into woodcuts and printed it, and his four horsemen gallop off the page together. Painters, weavers, glassmakers and printers have kept turning this book into pictures. Why does it lend itself to the eye, and what do the pictures uncover?

First, the name. The book opens, in the King James, "The Revelation of Jesus Christ." The Greek word there is apokalypsis: an uncovering, an unveiling. In the text, apocalypse doesn't mean disaster. It means a curtain pulled back. Second, the book is already a picture book. Again and again John says I saw, I beheld, I looked. In chapter six, as the seals open, the horses come one by one: white, red, black, and then this: "And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him." Colors, riders, crowns, scales. An artist barely has to invent anything. Third, every picture is a reading. Whoever makes one has to choose. Which scene? How frightening? Do the horsemen come one by one, as the text has them, or charge together, as Dürer drew them, a single wave thundering over the people below? Show the dragon, or the woman it can't destroy? Some artists dwelt on the terror. Some gave as much room to the river, the tree and the open city. A tapestry or a woodcut shows what its maker heard in the book, and often what the maker's own time feared and hoped. Fourth, why it matters. A picture can do what the book does: hold back the ordinary for a moment and uncover something. Some people meet Revelation first through an image, before they ever read a line of it. A pale horse on a print can make a reader go and look up chapter six.
screen: `AN IMAGE SENDS YOU TO THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one apocalypse artwork. Before the bell, find an image: Dürer's Four Horsemen, a panel of the Angers tapestry, or any picture from Revelation in a Bible or a book. If you can't find one, picture the holy city with open gates from this week. Settle, and breathe. Look for the whole sit. Don't read about it. Just look. Find one detail you missed at first glance. Then ask what the artist was afraid of, and what the artist hoped for. If you pray, you can let the image become a prayer without words. The bell holds the time.
The apocalypse in art. Tapestry, woodcut, paint and glass: artists turning John's I saw into pictures, each one a reading of the book.
Your line: art unveils. Today, look at one picture, poster or window slowly, and ask what it uncovers that you'd walked past before. Day one thousand three hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Christians have pictured Revelation in tapestries, illuminated manuscripts, woodcuts, paintings and stained glass, and some churches and museums display these works for people to look at and pray with.

match.prompt: Revelation in art — tap the pairs.

myth: the word apocalypse means the destruction of the world
the book's own word, apokalypsis, means an uncovering: "The Revelation of Jesus Christ."
in Revelation 6, the rider on the pale horse is named Death
"his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him."
in the text, the four horsemen charge out together
they come one by one, as the seals open. Dürer drew them riding together.

fork.setup: you're an artist asked to show the pale horse of Revelation 6 to people who can't read. if you follow the text, what must its rider have?
options: the name Death, with Hell following him.
fork.reveal: "his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him." the bow and crown belong to the white horse's rider; the balances to the black.

original.note: Greek: an uncovering, an unveiling. the first word of the book of Revelation.

trapdoor: what you thought: apocalypse art is just fire and monsters.
what it means: artists turned John's "I saw" into pictures, choosing which scenes to show, and how much terror and hope to give them.
what a scholar hears: apokalypsis, uncovering. the book is already a run of visions in words, so every image of it is also a reading of it.

notes: Claims rule: no dates, lengths or panel counts for the Angers Apocalypse Tapestry or Dürer's Apocalypse series. The tapestry is described as wool, in a castle in Angers, long enough to walk beside; Dürer's horsemen as riding together. Confirm these descriptions.
'Some artists dwelt on the terror. Some gave as much room to the river, the tree and the open city': a general claim about art; confirm or soften.
'Some people meet Revelation first through an image': general claim; confirm.
'Often what the maker's own time feared and hoped' is a general art-historical observation; confirm.
Revelation 6: white horse rider has a bow and crown (6:2), black horse rider a pair of balances (6:5). Confirm the fork reveal.
Original: ἀποκάλυψις, the first word of Revelation 1:1 in Greek. Confirm.
